source: Wang and Sun (2025) Unable to Forget: Proactive Interference Reveals Working Memory Limits in LLMs (v2, section 5 mitigations)
finding: Natural-language 'forget the old updates' and 'pay attention to what follows' prompts did not fix proactive interference. The per-key forget prompt moved the errors to the spot where the instruction was placed.
numbers: Per-key forget prompt: less than 10 percentage points gain over baseline at 100 updates. A relevance meta-prompt had a negative effect on gpt-4.1-mini. Models in the mitigation figures include gpt-4.1-mini, gemini-2.0-flash, claude-3.5-sonnet.
quote: forget or focus do not effectively reduce interference
limits: Prompt-only suppression is weak in this task. Tested on non-reasoning models only.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: a plain 'ignore old values' line is not enough for our agent. Keep the state structure, not the instruction, as the fix.

source: Wang and Sun (2025) Unable to Forget, section 5.3 Mock-QA-reset
finding: A fake user question plus a fake assistant answer that lists the current values of all keys, inserted 120 updates before the final query, partly cut interference. It works by turning old updates into a closed, answered batch.
numbers: Inserted 120 updates before the final query. Gain described as partial; exact per-model percentages not read from the figure text.
limits: Authors call it an ad hoc hack. Reasoning models were excluded from the study. No equal-token comparison.
agent_relevance: This is a restate-the-current-state step with a task boundary. It supports gap 1 and 5 in direction. It is not a test of overwrite versus append at equal tokens.

source: Wang and Sun (2025) Unable to Forget, scope of models
finding: Reasoning models were left out of the size and context regression because they were too slow. So the published decline curve does not cover frontier reasoning models.
numbers: Regression on open models only: size class t=3.03, p=0.005, N=30; context length t=-0.144, p=0.886; R2=0.261.
quote: Reasoning models were excluded because their more extensive inference processes caused latency to exceed 200 seconds per task
limits: The reason given is practical (latency over 200 seconds per task), not a finding about reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 stays open for 2026 reasoning models on PI-LLM. Do not assume the log-linear curve holds for them.

source: giantfish-fly (2025) LLMs-First-Task dataset card for PI-LLM
finding: The authors of the PI benchmark state that GPT-5, Grok-4, Gemini 2.5 Pro, DeepSeek, Mistral and Llama 4 also show the log-linear decline in last-value retrieval, and that humans stay near 99 percent.
numbers: Humans near 99%+. No per-model numbers on the card. On the value-length test GPT-5 and Grok-4 decline similarly to GPT-2 (authors' words).
limits: Dataset card, an author claim, not peer reviewed. Reasoning setting of these models is not stated.
agent_relevance: Weak partial answer to gap 3: the authors say 2025 frontier models decline too. Needs our own run with numbers.

source: Huang, Sun, Wang, Dredze (2026) On the Failure of Latent State Persistence in Large Language Models (v5)
finding: Models cannot hold a hidden number or hidden variable unless it is written into the context. Reasoning tokens act as a scratchpad that bypasses the limit, so working memory in LLMs is the written trace.
numbers: 17 models. Hidden-state-persistence rate under chain-of-thought (count of 150): GPT-4o-mini 5 (3.3%), GPT-4o-2024-05 26 (17.3%), GPT-4o-2024-08 31 (20.7%), Llama-3.3-70B 25 (16.7%), Qwen2.5-7B 49 (32.7%), Qwen2.5-72B 37 (24.7%), DeepSeek-V3 48 (32.0%). Reasoning models, five values in table order: 75/150 (50.0), 145/150 (96.7), 54/150 (36.0), 135/150 (90.0), 150/150 (100); mapping to o1-mini, o3-mini, o4-mini, QwQ, R1 is inferred from table order.
quote: internal CoT ... do not bridge the LSP gap
limits: Tasks are a number-guessing game and a variable-transformation task, not n-back. Row mapping of the last five numbers inferred from pdftotext order.
agent_relevance: Supports the schema rule that every live variable must be written out. Covers gap 3 for o-series and R1 (2025), not 2026 models. Internal CoT alone does not give latent persistence.

source: Liang, Zhu, Wang, Zhou (2026) Can Vision Replace Text in Working Memory? Evidence from Spatial n-Back in Vision-Language Models
finding: Small Qwen2.5 models do better with text-rendered grids than image-rendered grids on d' and accuracy. Nominal 2-back and 3-back often act like a comparison to the most recent item, not the instructed lag. Grid size changes the number of recent repeats and so the error pattern.
numbers: Table 1 location recognition accuracy (200 random grids): Qwen2.5-7B text 80.50/73.00/62.00/55.00; Qwen2.5-VL-7B text 70.00/63.50/58.00/53.50; Qwen2.5-VL-7B vision 78.50/82.00/77.00/80.50 (four columns; column meaning not verified).
limits: Only 7B-scale open models; no frontier model; short paper.
agent_relevance: Another sign that n-back scores mix lag-following with recency shortcuts (agrees with Gong 2026). Gap 3: still no 2026 frontier n-back numbers.

source: Hou et al. (2026) CogBattery: Human-Referenced Evaluation of Cognitive Task Behavior and Structure in Language Models (v2)
finding: 54 open-weight models on 13 paradigms including digit span, 2-back with lures and operation span. Models show the human lure effect but also false-alarm on ordinary non-targets.
numbers: 2-back ordinary non-target false alarms exceed human by .257 [.159,.341]; excess in 39 of 54 models and 19 of 23 families. Of 32 n-back gate passers, 19 have balanced accuracy below .60 and only 3 (all native-thinking models) reach .80. 702 cells, 366,606 records.
limits: Open-weight models only. No per-model table was read.
agent_relevance: Part of gaps 3 and 5: only thinking models clear n-back well, and lure false alarms are a general weakness across families.

source: Hou et al. (2026) CogBattery, structure and scale
finding: Model scores on the 13 tasks share one scale-related dimension. Groupings by cognitive construct (for example working memory) predict held-out families no better than random groups of the same size.
numbers: Adding PC2 to PC1 gives no reliable gain (3.17% [-1.53, 15.73]%). Five predefined groups versus random: gain -2.02% [-5.10, .48]% on 12 key endpoints. On 7 of 13 tasks more than 70% of models lie over 1 human SD from the human mean, not shrinking consistently with size.
limits: Panel of 54 open models; correlations are across models, not within a model.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: with 54 models there is no sign that 'working memory tasks' form a distinct factor. The 10-model n-back to reasoning link in Xiong looks like a general scale effect. Training compute was not controlled here either.

source: Emura and Sugawara (2026) A Dual-Task Paradigm to Investigate Sentence Comprehension Strategies in Language Models
finding: Adding an arithmetic task to a comprehension task pushes GPT-4o, o3-mini and o4-mini toward plausibility-based answers, as in humans. o3-mini and o4-mini stay near 100 percent in all conditions.
numbers: Mean plausible-minus-implausible accuracy gap 0.064 in dual task versus 0.025 single and 0.035 noisy single (as reported for the pooled case). Seven models tested incl. GPT-4.1, DeepSeek-V3, Llama-3.3, Gemma-3; only conditions with at least 80% single-task accuracy kept.
limits: Sentence task with arithmetic addends; temperature 0; human control uses easy 1-digit sums.
agent_relevance: A dual-task cost exists in LLMs but is small for reasoning models. Test a parallel duty on our agent before assuming a cost.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems (v3)
finding: Splitting work across several agents at matched total token budget is not generally better. It helps only when the task decomposes; it hurts sequential tasks and tool-heavy tasks.
numbers: 260 configurations, 6 benchmarks, 5 architectures, 3 LLM families; matched mean 4,800 reasoning tokens per trial. Relative to single agent: +80.8% (Finance Agent, centralized) to -70.0% (PlanCraft, independent). SWE-bench Verified single agent 0.522; Hybrid -2.1%, Centralized -3.1%, Decentralized -5.4%, Independent -14.9%. Mean MAS change over all: -0.3% (95% CI -58.7% to +77.2%). Cross-validated R2 0.373 to 0.413.
limits: Tool-using agentic benchmarks, not working-memory tasks. The single-agent arm has no special structured-notes condition.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 largely answered: load splitting alone is not a default win at equal tokens. Use it only for decomposable parallel parts; a single agent with a good state is the baseline to beat.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Scaling Agent Systems, capability saturation and checking
finding: Coordination gives diminishing or negative returns once the single-agent baseline is strong. Agents without a central checker pass on more errors.
numbers: Hybrid overhead 515% versus Centralized 285%; Hybrid -2.4% versus Centralized, gap 1.1%, t(178)=0.61, p=0.542 (not significant). Finance: Anthropic centralized +127.5% (0.636 vs 0.280), Google centralized +164.3% (0.740).
limits: The 45% threshold seen in secondary summaries was not checked in the text read.
agent_relevance: Do not add a second agent for memory reasons. Add a checker only where the single agent is weak.

source: Tang et al. (2026, ICML) Do Language Models Track Entities Across State Changes?
finding: LMs do not update a state step by step. They gather the relevant information at the last token. Deleting an item works through a fragile global 'remove tag' that weakens over a long context.
numbers: 300 sentences per failure scenario, greedy decoding. Degeneration rate (item wrongly stays removed), CodeLlama-13B / Llama-3.1-70B: no-op remove 0.84/0.49; shared-label objects 0.56/0.27; re-introducing a removed object 0.62/0.01. Zeroing the tag recovers the item: intervention success 0.66/0.59, 0.73/0.74, 0.24/0.50.
limits: Open models (13B, 70B), toy box-object language, no frontier reasoning models. The 70B almost solves re-introduction (0.01).
agent_relevance: Gap 1: 'retire a stale value' is a weak operation inside the model, so an explicit rewrite that drops the old value from the written state is safer than a REMOVE statement. A direct overwrite-versus-append test at equal tokens is still missing.

source: Pougeon, Camos, Belletier, Barrouillet (2024) Quantifying resource sharing in working memory
finding: Humans doing storage and processing together keep about half or more of each single-task span. The sum of the two retained shares is above 100 percent, which a pure shared-resource or pure time-sharing view does not predict.
numbers: Exp 1 (N=24): span 6.42 letters [5.90,6.93], processing span 5.88 digits; dual-task memory accuracy .88 to .66, processing .83 to .58; combined 124% [114,134]. Exp 2 with concurrent articulation: memory span 3.77; storage 45%, processing 61%, combined 107% [101,112].
limits: Letter span plus digit judgement; small student samples; authors are from the TBRS group.
agent_relevance: Gaps 6 and 10: a second duty costs a human roughly a third to a half of each task, not all of it. Measure the same ratio for the agent (state kept plus task done).

source: Barrouillet, Bernardin, Camos (2004) Time constraints and resource sharing in adults' working memory spans (abstract)
finding: TBRS model: processing and maintenance share attention; memory traces decay when attention is switched away; retrievals form a bottleneck. Span depends on cognitive load, the ratio of retrieval time to total time.
numbers: 7 experiments show span varies with cognitive load (number of retrievals divided by time allowed).
limits: Only the abstract was read. The decay assumption is contested by Oberauer's group (titles seen: 'No evidence for temporal decay in working memory' 2009; 'Evidence against decay in verbal working memory' 2013), not opened.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: an LLM has no decay, so TBRS timing maps only to token budget. Treat refresh as 'rewrite the live state', not as timing.

source: Vergauwe, Souza, Langerock, Oberauer (2025) The effect of instructed refreshing on working memory
finding: A refreshing boost depends on the number of refreshing steps, not their duration, which fits a selection account. Some results were less robust than expected.
numbers: Number of refreshing steps affected recall; duration did not. Sample sizes not extracted.
limits: Authors say the effect is limited to certain task parameters.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: supports 'refresh = select the item again', which is what restating the relevant item does. Refresh count is the lever, not time.

source: Dames, Li, Frischkorn, Oberauer (2025) Removing information from working memory with a delay: effective but not beneficial
finding: Humans can remove an item after the fact and memory for it falls (removal cost), but the other items do not gain (no removal benefit). Immediate removal does give a benefit, by helping later encoding of new items.
limits: Letter updating plus directed forgetting; no retroactive benefit for stored content.
agent_relevance: Gap 1: even for humans, retiring a stale value late does not free the others. Retire a value when it is replaced, not in a later clean-up pass.

source: Oberauer and colleagues (2026) Removing information from working memory versus long-term memory (Forget For Now, but Remember Later)
finding: Words told to be removed from working memory were later remembered worse than words kept. People could not remove items from WM while keeping them in long-term memory.
numbers: Final experiment: participants compromised, removing less effectively and failing to remember better. Sample sizes not extracted.
limits: Abstract-level reading for the design; author list not verified.
agent_relevance: A removal step has a side effect on later recall. A retired value should be copied to a separate log if it may be needed later.
